articles.title: Authoritarian orientations and the contestation of liberal self-determination: Cross-national evidence from 30 countries
articles.authors: Heiko Giebler, Lukas Antoine, Rasmus Ollroge
articles.abstract: In contrast to expectations of global liberal convergence, liberal values and institutions are increasingly contested. This study investigates whether core liberal conditions for self-determination are likewise subject to contestation and how this varies across societal contexts. Drawing from liberal theory, we identify five enabling conditions for self-determination: physical well-being, basic economic security, learning and personal growth, moral equality, and influence on political decision-making. These conditions differ in their degree of ‘liberal uniqueness’, with the latter two representing distinctly liberal ideals. Using original survey data from over 45,000 respondents across 30 countries, we examine how authoritarian orientations – conceptualised as preferences for authority, conformity, order, and security – relate to support for these conditions. Such orientations are consistently and negatively associated with uniquely liberal conditions, especially moral equality and political influence. In contrast, there is no meaningful relationship with basic economic security and a positive association with physical well-being. Preferences for learning and personal growth fall in between. These associations vary with levels of societal modernisation; in more modernised societies, the gap between respondents with stronger and weaker authoritarian orientations grows wider, with the strongest widening observed for the uniquely liberal conditions. Our findings suggest that authoritarian orientations are linked to different understandings of self-determination. These competing visions of what it means to live freely are more polarised in modern societies. Recognising this divergence helps to better understand the normative foundations of contemporary societal conflicts across diverse countries.

articles.title: Digital turnout mobilization: Enhancing voter turnout with digital messaging
articles.authors: Kasper M. Hansen, Esther Ejrnæs Bastholm
articles.abstract: Voter turnout is declining across Europe, raising concerns about democratic legitimacy and prompting a search for effective mobilization strategies. The new digital era has transformed the landscape for political communication, making it possible to mobilize voters through direct digital messages. These messages have proven to be a low-cost and easily scalable tool, capable of reaching millions of voters efficiently and with broad coverage. We synthesize existing evidence through a comprehensive meta-analysis of voter mobilization experiments from the past decade that apply digital messages as a Get-Out-The-Vote (GOTV) tool. The analysis assesses the overall effectiveness of digital messaging in increasing turnout, with particular attention to its potential for engaging marginalized groups and promoting participatory equality. Second, we present results from a new population-wide GOTV experiment conducted during the 2024 European Parliament election in Denmark – the first to apply digital messages to the entire electorate. The intervention increased turnout by 0.5 percentage points. By using year-of-birth bins to estimate effects across all age cohorts and disaggregating the immigrant category into Western and non-Western subpopulations, we can examine previously unexplored in-depth heterogeneous effects. We find that digital messages consistently have positive effects on turnout, including among marginalized voters.

articles.title: How experiential knowledge becomes evidence in lawmaking through consultations with incarcerated people
articles.authors: Kati Rantala, Maija Helminen, Mika Simonen, Susanna Lundell
articles.abstract: Experiential knowledge, grounded in lived experience, is increasingly recognized as an important source of evidence in policy making and legislative drafting. Yet questions remain about how knowledge derived from consultations with affected individuals can legitimately inform broader lawmaking. This article examines how experiential knowledge from targeted consultations with incarcerated individuals is transformed into context-specific legislative knowledge through the interplay of propositional system knowledge, procedural knowledge of navigating the prison system, and implicit analogical reasoning. Drawing on consultation memoranda and a draft Bill produced during the reform of the Finnish Imprisonment Act, we analyse consultations concerning incarcerated individuals’ use of communication technologies to manage essential practical matters beyond prison under conditions of administrative burden. We first construct a narrative from the consultees’ propositional and procedural experiential knowledge and then examine how this knowledge was incorporated into legislative arguments alongside official expert knowledge. Our analysis shows that the draft Bill employed implicit analogical reasoning to transform procedural knowledge of navigating the prison system into propositional claims applicable to broader prison populations sharing similar contexts, institutional routines, and practical needs. By demonstrating how analogical reasoning links propositional and procedural knowledge to generate context-specific generalizations, the article offers a novel conceptual framework for understanding how experiential knowledge can become legitimate evidence in lawmaking. We suggest that this approach is applicable to other institutional settings characterized by standardized living conditions, shared procedures, and common systems of navigation.

articles.title: When Crises Entrench Gendered Power: Male Elite Adaptation in the Ugandan Parliament
articles.authors: Amanda Clayton, Alyssa Heinze, Cecilia Josefsson, Pär Zetterberg
articles.abstract: Recent scholarship argues that crises can create opportunities for women's political leadership. Yet crises also create opportunities for male political elites to adapt strategically to preserve their power. We develop and test a theory of crisis‐induced adaptation, whereby male political elites respond by shifting political attention toward crisis dimensions that reinforce their authority. We examine this theory using the Ugandan Parliament's response to COVID‐19, a health crisis in a policy domain traditionally associated with women. Using the complete corpus of parliamentary debates from 1998 to 2022 and text‐as‐data analyses, we find no evidence that COVID‐19 reduced gender inequalities in legislative speech. Instead, the pandemic widened them. Men's dominance in legislative speech grew as they increasingly framed the pandemic through traditionally masculine policy domains—the economy and national security—rather than public health. Rather than opening space for women, crises can provide men with new opportunities to entrench political dominance.

articles.title: Privileged Franchise and the Political Representation of Elites: Evidence From Denmark
articles.abstract: Democratization, via franchise extension, can reduce traditional elite representation and power. We study whether autocratization similarly increases the representation of these elites. We use the case of Denmark from 1849 to 1915. A constitutional change in 1866 created a privileged franchise to the upper chamber of the parliament weighted towards the wealthy and rural areas, while leaving the electoral rules to the lower chamber unchanged. Using MP‐year level data, we apply a difference‐in‐difference approach to study whether this autocratizing reform increased the representation of Danish elites in the upper chamber relative to the lower chamber. We find that this reform indeed increased the share of traditional elites in the upper chamber of the parliament such as the nobility and landed estate owners, including those with political‐dynastic ties, and arguably therefore the nature of democratic representation in 19th century Denmark.

articles.title: Navigating conflicts in refugee shelters: decolonial everyday peace and humanitarian constraints
articles.abstract: Refugee shelters often become sites of conflict and violence. Grounded in refugees’ lived experiences and situated knowledges, this article introduces the framework of Decolonial Everyday Peace in Refugee Shelters to examine how residents prevent and respond to conflicts while navigating and contesting coloniality in micro-level peacebuilding. Drawing on a 6-month ethnographic fieldwork with Ukrainian refugees in a Warsaw shelter, the article discusses five everyday peace practices developed through the research: avoidance, strategic distraction, engagement, support seeking, and grounded resignation. The analysis shows how they unfold within, rather than beyond, the tensions of shelter life, embodying agency while remaining constrained by coloniality, including the shelter’s top-down peacebuilding approach, which limits possibilities for everyday peace. Yet, refugees also create spaces of coexistence, unsettling, however temporarily, colonial hierarchies. Decolonial everyday peace thus emerges not as an idealized end-state, but as a plural, situated, and unfinished process, continually constructed and reshaped through refugees’ everyday interactions.

The Synthetic Imputation Approach: Using LLMs to Generate Synthetic Texts for Underrepresented Categories in Supervised Classification Tasks
articles.abstract: Annotated text data are central to many empirical applications in political science, yet many annotation tasks involve categories that are sparsely populated. These low- N categories pose problems for both encoder-only and decoder-only (generative) Transformer large language models (LLMs), leading to low performance, biased evaluation and measurement error in downstream analyses. This article introduces the synthetic imputation approach, a targeted method for expanding sparse categories while remaining consistent with the category-defining content of the human-coded examples. The approach uses a generative LLM to produce additional texts for underrepresented categories by conditioning on small, rotating subsets of human-coded examples. Rather than paraphrasing or replacing the original data, synthetic imputation adds informative variation only where data are thin. I evaluate the approach using both encoder-only and decoder-only LLM classifiers across multiple political science applications. The results show that synthetic imputation substantially improves performance and evaluation stability in sparse settings, recovering full-sample performance once a modest number of true observations is available, with limited and predictable overfitting at very low levels of N .

Democracy and the Politics of Attention in the Digital Age
articles.abstract: In the digital age, attention has become a major issue of public concern. The emergence of various contemporary phenomena – including new digital architectures, new ways of monetizing them, and nefarious actors who have co-opted them – have led many people to argue that our attention is being stolen, fractured, and even traded on the open market. But, while these claims are becoming increasingly prevalent, attention remains an understudied concept in democratic theory. In this paper I work to pull out the relationship between attention and democratic politics in order to help us understand and contend with what is being called the “crisis of attention”. Primarily using the works of William James and Erving Goffman as a roadmap, I argue that it is through attentional fields that participants in democracies establish and negotiate the epistemic terrain from which possible actions are drawn. The upshot of this argument is that attentional fields can be a key resource towards the mobilization of democratic agency, but the erosion or manipulation of attentional fields can also be a vehicle through which democratic agency can be fractured, altered, or distorted.

articles.title: King’s Equality
articles.abstract: In a 1962 speech, Martin Luther King Jr. distinguished between a “stagnant equality of sameness” and a “constructive equality of oneness.” Scholars have rarely paused over this distinction, presuming King’s equality to be a mere extension of liberal or Christian moral equality. This article argues instead that King advances a distinctive idea of equality, one that refigures his understanding of politics. His equality begins not with future-focused reforms that seek to equalize various forms of power but instead with acknowledging specific realities that already equally bind us: our dependence on others to make sense of who we are, our inescapable historical indebtedness, and the tragic and limited nature of human understanding and action. To acknowledge these facts is not resignation; it is political work. King’s equality reorients politics away from power understood as mastery and control, and toward a practice of humility and awareness, constructively making different forms of political relation and action possible. Recovering this neglected strand of King’s thought offers a new way to understand equality—as an ongoing relation to reality—as well as a new image of King as a political realist.

articles.title: The link between three smartphone school policies and students’ mental health: a growth trajectory approach
articles.authors: Lara Schreurs, Robyn Vanherle, Jana Vereecke, Lise-Marie Nassen, Laura Vandenbosch, Kathleen Beullens
articles.abstract: Amid growing concerns about smartphones and students’ mental health, schools worldwide are introducing smartphone policies, often without evidence on their effectiveness. This longitudinal study examines how three naturally implemented policies (full restrictions, partial restrictions allowing use during lunchbreak, partial restrictions allowing use during lunch, and afternoon break) relate to mental health across one school year (up to seven waves). Differences were observed at the first measurement wave (two months after implementation): Students in the full-restriction school reported highest depressive symptoms and anxiety. Differences in life satisfaction were also observed without a clear pattern across policy types. Growth trajectory analyses revealed no significant differences in mental health changes over time. Yet, within schools, both the full-restrictions and the lunchbreak school showed increases in depressive symptoms. Life satisfaction decreased slightly in the lunchbreak school. These findings suggest that smartphone restrictions are not a simple solution to youth mental health challenges.

articles.title: Strategic divergences: Comparing national approaches to critical raw materials
articles.abstract: Critical raw materials have become central in policy debates due to their importance for economic growth and national security, as well as the vulnerabilities arising from the geographic concentration of their supply chains. Alongside intensifying geopolitical tensions, these factors have prompted many countries to adopt national strategies aimed at mitigating supply-chain risks or securing a position in the expanding global market. Although these strategies tend to share similar objectives, they differ across several important dimensions, depending on the priorities emphasized by policymakers during their formulation. In this article, we introduce an analytical framework to map and explain such divergences. We apply this framework to examine national strategies on critical raw materials developed in 23 jurisdictions worldwide since 2008. Combining qualitative content analysis with descriptive statistics, we investigate the evolution of these strategies over time and identify the main drivers behind variation in national approaches to critical raw materials governance.

Governing knowledge through program architecture: strategic valorization, infrastructural integration, and the autonomy-steering settlement in Horizon Europe after 2027
articles.abstract: European research framework programs have long governed knowledge through architecture rather than through funding instruments alone. The proposed post-2027 reconfiguration of Horizon Europe is therefore interpreted as a recalibration of an established knowledge-governance architecture. The article conceptualizes program architecture as the formal-organizational configuration of a public program: the arrangement of pillars, domains, budgetary couplings, coordination mechanisms, eligibility rules, steering devices, valorization pathways, and accountability routines through which authority, participation, and access to resources are structured. This definition positions program architecture as a meso-level mechanism of policy steering between individual instruments and broader governance regimes. Drawing on qualitative document analysis and cross-temporal comparison of Horizon Europe 2021–2027 and the proposed 2028–2034 framework, the article identifies five interrelated shifts. First, the proposed Pillar II “Competitiveness and Society” more closely links societal relevance to strategic, industrial, and technological priorities. Second, ERA and widening move from horizontal and partly compensatory support toward infrastructural integration. Third, dispersed innovation support is consolidated into a strategically governed valorization pipeline connecting co-creation, industry-academia alignment, standardization, scale-up, strategic technologies, and sovereignty. Fourth, budgetary coupling with competitiveness-oriented investment structures anchors strategic selectivity. Fifth, performance steering is strengthened through high-visibility initiatives, milestones, and accountability routines that make program results more traceable to political priorities. The article shows how program architecture filters societal relevance, inclusion, and valorization without formally abolishing scientific autonomy. It thereby explains how public programs steer knowledge by structuring the routes through which research becomes fundable, visible, valorizable, and politically relevant.

articles.title: Praise, rent, and the platform: Substack and the enclosure of blog culture
articles.abstract: This article situates Substack within the platformisation of blogging and the enclosure of cultural production within proprietary infrastructures. Tracing the genealogy of blogging as a decentralised practice that carried within it the seeds of citizen journalism and informal intellectual life, I argue that Substack does not restore an apparently lost cultural practice but renegotiates and interpolates blogging into a platformised logic. Framed as a return to independent, writer-led publishing, Substack instead, as I argue, renders free-labour interaction as a source of rent. I analyse the rhetoric and revolving discourse around Substack’s internal curatorial project, ‘The Substack Post’. Drawing on Jodi Dean’s account of blogs as displaced mediators alongside theories of digital labour and platform capitalism, and approaching Substack as a simultaneously platformised and infrastructuralised formation, I argue that praise operates as a platform-specific form of commodity fetishism, animating the platform while obscuring the labour relations that sustain it.

articles.title: Platformed affective withdrawal: Quiet quitting and the refusal of gendered emotional labour on TikTok
articles.abstract: This article examines #quietquitting on TikTok as a platform-mediated articulation of gendered affective withdrawal. While organisational research interprets quiet quitting as reduced discretionary effort or declining work engagement, this study examines how quiet quitting is articulated as a digitally circulated refusal of feminised emotional labour. Drawing on feminist theories of affective labour and critical platform studies, the analysis explores how workers renegotiate expectations of emotional availability within algorithmically structured visibility regimes. The study is based on a qualitative-dominant mixed-methods analysis of 586 TikTok videos shared under #quietquitting between 2020 and 2026. Combining thematic discourse analysis with descriptive engagement indicators, the findings show that creators frequently frame quiet quitting as a refusal of unpaid relational mediation, emotional management, and workplace care. The article introduces the concept of platformed affective withdrawal to explain how narratives of workplace disengagement circulate through algorithmic visibility systems that amplify and individualise gendered labour inequalities.

articles.title: Stress and self-efficacy under artificial intelligence disruption: A mixed-methods study on the usage of artificial intelligence among Finnish workers
articles.authors: Atte Oksanen, Teo Keipi, Moona Heiskari, Iina Savolainen
articles.abstract: Rapid workplace integration of artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping work practices and challenging employees’ self-efficacy and well-being. This mixed-methods study examines these experiences using national survey data ( N = 2109) and qualitative interviews ( N = 54) with Finnish workers. Frequent AI use, AI-induced identity threat, and organizational AI deployment are associated with higher AI strain, whereas AI self-efficacy relates to frequent use, positive AI attitudes, and subjective well-being. Identity threat moderated several of these associations, highlighting the role of professional identity in AI-related experiences. Analysis drawing on Greimas’ semiotic modalities (must, can, know, and want) explains how these patterns are interpreted and negotiated in practice, revealing tensions between perceived self-efficacy and pressures to integrate AI. AI use was often described as voluntary. However, participants anticipated increasing competence demands and responsibility. The findings emphasize the need for organizational strategies that address identity-related challenges and support employee well-being in AI-driven work transformations.

No vote for recovery? Local electoral effects of NextGeneration European Union funds in Spain
articles.abstract: Do European Union (EU) funds affect voting behavior in local elections? Following the COVID-19 crisis, the EU launched an unprecedented financial effort through the NextGeneration EU program, channeling billions of euros to support reforms and investments across different policy areas in all Member States. Using several empirical designs, including an observational, a Regression Discontinuity Design and a Difference-in-Difference strategy, this article investigates whether these investments influenced electoral outcomes in Spain’s 2023 municipal elections. Despite the scale and policy relevance of the program and the opportunity to claim credit by mayors, we find no evidence that local allocations of recovery funds increased support for incumbent parties. These null results contrast with earlier works from other European funding programs, which have often yielded electoral rewards under favorable conditions, such as high visibility, political alignment, or clear attribution. In Spain, however, the political impact of NextGeneration EU spending appears to be absent, possibly due to the low visibility of projects, the complexity of fund administration, or the lack of clear political ownership. Our findings highlight the limits of top-down economic interventions in generating local political returns and call for a closer examination of the conditions under which supranational spending shapes electoral behavior.

articles.title: AI politics and regulation in the European Parliament: Ideological divides and policy convergence amid generative AI’s ascent
articles.authors: Étienne Proulx, Jacob Steve, Arnaud Beaulé, Shannon Dinan, Yannick Dufresne
articles.abstract: This study examines how European parliamentarians frame artificial intelligence in plenary speech. It also assesses how these frames map onto partisan divisions. Analyzing 666 interventions in the European Parliament (2014–2024), it shows that frames of artificial intelligence follow traditional ideological cleavages, with right-leaning parliamentarians deploying techno-optimistic frames that foreground economic innovation while left-leaning parliamentarians frame the technology through concerns about social risks and employment impacts. Thematic context also shapes framing. When interventions address economic competitiveness, optimistic frames increase significantly across the political spectrum. The findings reveal a cross-partisan consensus in favor of regulating artificial intelligence, regardless of the frames deployed. This suggests that political contestation centers not on the principle of regulatory intervention, but on its modalities and objectives. Emerging technologies are absorbed into existing ideological frameworks while generating zones of strategic convergence when economic and normative considerations align.

articles.title: Geographic representation and information capacity in the European Union
articles.abstract: The European Union prioritizes geographic representation of member states when recruiting staff. Many assume a trade-off between expertise and geographic representation, where the former increases capacity and the latter increases legitimacy. However, this article provides evidence that geographic representation can enhance bureaucratic information capacity. Using the European Commission’s Directorate-General for Economic and Financial Affairs as a case study, I provide evidence that increasing representation of bureaucrats from a member state is associated with higher accuracy in that state’s economic forecasts. This association decreases as member state representation within the Commission increases. These findings suggest that prioritizing geographic balance in the European Union need not come at the cost of information capacity, and may in fact improve it.

articles.title: Integrating care into growth regimes: the politics of social reproduction and hybridity in Japan and Korea
articles.abstract: This study integrates the care economy as a constitutive dimension of growth regime theory, bridging production-centred and reproduction-centred approaches to comparative political economy. It theorizes three conditional mechanisms linking care and growth and specifies the political and institutional conditions under which these mechanisms generate positive-sum integration or trade-off dynamics. Applying a comparative institutional analysis to Japan and South Korea, the study examines how care-growth linkages operate within hybrid growth regimes that combine a manufacturing-export core with elements of financialization and innovation-driven services. This East Asian hybridity is conceptualized as intra-regime recombination, differing from other mixed types based on territorial dualism or regime transition. Despite recent care expansion, both care economies remain partially familialized and significantly market-based, and the three mechanisms are only incompletely activated. Together, these findings advance a framework for analysing care as a politically conditioned and regime-specific dimension of growth, extending comparative political economy beyond its production-centred foundations.

articles.title: Robot-based automation and new firm formation: the role of formal human capital development
articles.abstract: Industrial robots are reshaping manufacturing, yet their role in new firm formation remains underexplored. Robot-based automation reinforces incumbent advantages while reconfiguring tasks in ways that may create opportunities for entrepreneurial entry. Formal human capital development can renew knowledge and skills to recognize and pursue opportunities. Drawing on the task-based theory of technological change and the Varieties of Capitalism framework, we examine how the intensity of robot-based automation relates to new firm formation and the moderating role of formal human capital development in this relationship. Using 2006–16 panel data for seven industries across thirteen European countries, we find that robot density is associated with lower new firm formation, while formal adult education and training relate positively to entry, though its moderating role varies across institutional and industry contexts. Entrepreneurial adjustment to automation depends not only on technology, but also on institutional and industry characteristics conditioning the role of formal human capital development.

articles.title: Returns to Caring? Health and Well‐Being Effects of Subsidized Long‐Term Care
articles.authors: Joan Costa‐Font, Sergi Jiménez‐Martín, Cristina Vilaplana‐Prieto
articles.abstract: We estimate the health and well‐being effects of subsidized access to long‐term care (LTC). Our analysis exploits the staggered implementation of Spain's 2007 System of Autonomy and Care for Dependent People (SAAD), which expanded publicly funded and universal LTC subsidies and supports, as well as its subsequent reform. Using two decades of administrative and survey data and leveraging exogenous regional and individual‐level variation in program exposure, we find that access to SAAD benefits reduces the care receiver's depressive symptoms by approximately 10 percentage points, increases its survival probability by 2.6–3 percentage points, and raises its life satisfaction by 0.24–0.50 scale points. Cost‐effectiveness estimates indicate that the implied cost per quality‐adjusted life year (QALY) gained lies below commonly accepted efficiency thresholds for public health spending in Europe. These findings document sizeable health returns and efficiency gains from publicly subsidized LTC provision.

articles.title: Means‐Tested Public Transportation Subsidies: Causal Evidence and Implications
articles.authors: Seoyoon Ahn, Matthew Freedman, David Phillips, Atheendar Venkataramani
articles.abstract: This paper evaluates the effects of a novel and large‐scale program in King County, Washington, that provides fare‐free public transportation to individuals with low incomes. Using both experimental and quasi‐experimental methods together with rich administrative and survey data, we find that providing free transit has very limited effects on mobility or downstream outcomes related to health and well‐being. We examine possible explanations for the modest effects, which contrast with findings from prior research. Our results suggest that changes in the external environment post‐COVID‐19 pandemic, including changes in norms around fare evasion, reduced the price elasticity of demand for travel by transit among individuals with low incomes.

articles.title: Revisiting the Carbon Lock-In: Outlining an Agenda on How Affective Polarization Constrains Climate Policy Making
articles.abstract: Carbon lock-in, the self-reinforcing inertia that perpetuates fossil fuel dependence, emerges from interdependent technological, institutional, economic, and behavioral factors. As climate policy has become increasingly polarized across advanced democracies, the role of affective polarization in reinforcing these barriers remains underexplored. This research agenda asks the following question: How and to what extent does affective polarization sustain the carbon lock-in? Drawing on social identity theory and the carbon lock-in literature, I propose a framework in which affective polarization operates as a cross-cutting process strengthening existing lock-in mechanisms through three pathways: (1) elite framing that activates both institutional distrust and out-group animosity toward pro-climate groups; (2) trust erosion linking vertical (elite–mass) and horizontal (mass–mass) polarization to sustained policy resistance; and (3) self-reinforcing feedback loops between polarizing rhetoric and mass resistance that persist across electoral cycles. Partisan identity sorting can transform climate policies into identity markers, turning otherwise reversible constraints into path-dependent barriers that persist even when policies are economically beneficial or technically effective. The agenda applies specifically to high-polarization contexts and calls for empirical investigation of these mechanisms and of depolarization interventions.

articles.title: Trade, Human Capital, and Income Risk,
articles.authors: Liuchun Deng, Pravin Krishna, Mine Z Senses, Jens Stegmaier
articles.abstract: In this paper, we study the causal relationship between trade exposure and individual income risk, with emphasis on the role of human capital. We use a rich worker-level longitudinal dataset from Germany spanning the period 1976-2012, and find industry trade exposure to be causally related to income risk: Imports increase risk and exports decrease risk in an economically significant manner. Importantly, there is a complex interplay between human capital and the linkage between trade and risk: On average, individuals with higher levels of industry- or occupation-specific human capital experience lower risk. However, an increase in industry net imports increases risk more for workers with higher levels of industry tenure. Although net imports are also associated with declines in the mean income of these workers, the estimated effect on income levels is economically small. Our welfare framework, which jointly considers both mean income and income risk, shows that the welfare consequences of trade exposure are quantitatively dominated by the risk channel.

articles.title: Conflict or Compromise? Theory and Evidence from Africa and Asia
articles.abstract: Civil wars are a recurring phenomenon undermining development in weak states. Faced with the possibility of costly conflict, why don’t leaders share power? I investigate the role of an unexplored commitment problem, both theoretically and empirically. The model features a leader who can appease challengers by sharing power, but doing so increases their effectiveness at launching a rebellion. I show that commitment worsens as the opposition becomes stronger, and derive testable non-monotonic implications of group strength on power-sharing and conflict. As challengers become stronger, the likelihood of inclusion (positive transfers) increases up to a threshold, beyond which the leader prefers to exclude an opposing group and face conflict. I test the model using data on politically relevant ethnic groups in Africa and Asia, their access to executive power, and on armed organizations that claim to represent them. I use within-country variation in population share to proxy for group strength. The empirical findings strongly accord with the predictions of the theory. I then structurally estimate the model parameters and explore policy-relevant counterfactuals, including the effects of democratization, changes in military capacity, financial aid, sanctions, and quotas.

articles.title: Managing Groundwater Salinization Toward Sustainability
articles.authors: Dongmei Han, Matthew J. Currell, Yoseph Yechieli, Ryan T. Bailey, Abhijit Mukherjee, Xuan Yu, Dawid Potrykus, Gerson Cardoso da Silva, Guoliang Cao, Yi Xiao, Zitun Wang, Adam Szymkiewicz, Pieter J. Stuyfzand, Seifu Kebede Gurmessa, Deqiang Mao, Lihe Yin
articles.abstract: Groundwater, a crucial freshwater source worldwide, is under threat of salinization due to the combined pressures of climate change and human activities, hindering sustainable development. This review explores both natural and anthropogenic sources and mechanisms of groundwater salinization (GWS). We describe the impacts of GWS on environmental and socioeconomic systems, highlighting the risks to agriculture, water quality, and public health. We also discuss monitoring and assessment techniques and knowledge gaps essential for effective management. We present successful case studies of interventions in seven countries, showcasing the feasibility and difficulty of effective management and mitigation strategies. Finally, we address sustainability challenges and outline future directions for research and policy, emphasizing the need for a paradigm shift from reactive management to proactive, holistic, and adaptive stewardship.

articles.title: A Review of Beyond GDP: History, Barriers, Opportunities, and Cautions
articles.authors: Joseph Eastoe, Ida Kubiszewski, Robert Costanza, Rutger Hoekstra, Annegeke Jansen, Peter Benczur, Kenneth Mulder, Richard Heys, Sandrine Dixson-Declève
articles.abstract: Gross domestic product (GDP) remains the dominant measure of economic progress, despite long-standing critiques including its failure to account for environmental sustainability, inequality, and social well-being. In the context of escalating climate breakdown and rising inequality, GDP is increasingly being recognized as an inadequate metric for national prosperity. This article reviews the growing movement toward alternative measures that prioritize sustainability, inclusion, and the well-being of humans and the rest of nature. Hundreds of alternatives exist, but recent research shows significant similarity among them, forming the basis for building a broad consensus. This review explores how academics and policy makers are responding to the limitations of standard national accounts and highlights broad public support for expanding economic indicators. This review also identifies the key barriers to be overcome in order to move beyond GDP—including vested interests, institutional buy-in, and the fragmentation of alternatives—and suggests strategies to address each. By examining these barriers and evaluating potential solutions within the current political landscape, this review contributes to the discourse on how national accounting systems can better evolve to reflect the goals of a just and sustainable economy embedded in society and the rest of nature.

articles.title: Governing Solar Geoengineering at Planetary Scale: Pipe Dream or Possibility?
articles.authors: Frank Biermann, Aarti Gupta, Rakhyun E. Kim, Florian Rabitz
articles.abstract: Solar geoengineering is being suggested by some scientists as a partial solution to the climate crisis. However, these hypothetical technologies to reflect parts of incoming sunlight back out into space pose significant governance challenges, due to their ecological risks, planetary scale, and long-term consequences. This review examines the literature on solar geoengineering governance since 2020, identifying three strands of debate. The first explores emerging research governance and institutional arrangements for potential future deployment. The second, critical, strand focuses instead on institutional pathways to prohibit such technologies. A third strand analyzes the debate itself, including through the lens of science and technology studies. While proposals for solar geoengineering are developed by small groups of researchers in industrialized countries, opposition is growing in the Global South, with governments from Africa and the Pacific calling for an international nonuse agreement. This growing resistance from vulnerable nations raises pressing moral and political questions about continuing research amid mounting global dissent.

articles.title: Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (OECMs) in Global Area-Based Conservation
articles.authors: Catherine M. Wensink, Daniel J. Ingram, Awantha Dissanayake, Nicola Weber, Julia E. Fa
articles.abstract: Other Effective Area-Based Conservation Measures (OECMs) are an emerging area-based conservation mechanism aspiring to achieve long-term and effective in situ biodiversity conservation outside traditional protected areas. Contributing toward several global biodiversity targets, they combine protection with sustainable land use and human development. This review analyzes spatial and temporal trends in OECM site designation (2010–2024), exploring governance frameworks, management, and ecological effectiveness in reducing biodiversity loss, addressing environmental change, and promoting sustainable development. Emphasis is placed on inclusivity of OECMs, particularly engagement of local communities and Indigenous Peoples in stewardship and decision-making, thereby enhancing social equity and cultural relevance. Academic and policy attention has centered on two areas: ( a ) refining the OECM framework, its definition, characteristics, and alignment with international goals (Section 3), and ( b ) evaluating governance, effectiveness, and national/subnational implementation (Section 4). While OECMs offer potential to expand global conservation, issues around governance and site-level outcomes remain underexplored and warrant attention (Section 5).

articles.title: Worlds Made Extractive: Black, Decolonial, and Feminist Geographies of Extractivism and Resistance
articles.abstract: Over the past two decades, scholars have reconceptualized extraction as ( a ) embedded within racial capitalism's systems of global, uneven accumulation and ( b ) a constitutive organizing principle of contemporary capitalism. Extractivism refers to contested discursive and material practices, governance technologies, and terrains of struggle rooted in racial capitalism which shape how people perceive and relate to the world. Extractive logics describes the ontological and epistemic structures through which extractivism renders differentiated subjects legible, governable, and exploitable. Extractive capitalism fosters dissent, consent, and acquiescence and by foregrounding the micropolitics of extractivism—labor, emotions, embodiment, endurance, care and domestic labor, and life-making practices—social scientists working differently within and across Marxist, Black, feminist, and Indigenous traditions show how people and more-than-human life inhabit and unsettle extractive logics. This review draws from transdisciplinary research in political economy-ecology that reinterprets slow dissent, refusal, and resurgence as world-making practices which reclaim time, land, emotion, and relationality against extractive capitalism.

articles.title: Who Should Read This Journal?
articles.authors: Arun Agrawal, Ashok Gadgil, Thomas P. Tomich, Diana Ürge-Vorsatz

articles.title: Expanded Urban Innovation for the Twenty-Second Century: From Cutting Emissions to Enabling Flourishing Lives on a Thriving Planet
articles.authors: Dennis Pamlin, Pourya Salehi, Massamba Thioye, Sascha Nick, Felix Creutzig, Ganesh Das, Jay Hennessy
articles.abstract: Cities are central to the climate challenge, but much research on urban climate action still focuses on emissions reductions within existing systems. This literature review assesses existing research and literature, including work on human-need-driven innovation for global sustainability and the export of globally sustainable solutions. Rather than limiting urban climate action to measures aimed at reaching zero emissions, the review examines an expanded urban innovation agenda in which cities are studied as incubators and exporters of innovations that support flourishing lives for all on a flourishing planet. The review synthesizes insights from sustainability transitions, sociotechnical systems, well-being economics, artificial intelligence, and brain science. Case studies from different cities illustrate how some urban innovation agendas are already shifting. The comparison highlights how a focus on flourishing lives can mobilize start-ups, youth, and public institutions, while addressing equity and positioning cities as actors in the next generation of urban climate action.

articles.title: Social Energy Futures in the Global South: Geographies, Concepts, and Praxis
articles.authors: Sofía Ávila-Calero, Ksenija Hanaček, Marcela Torres Wong, Tristan Partridge, Brototi Roy, Bruno Fornillo, Arnim Scheidel
articles.abstract: Socioenvironmental research highlights the key role of communities and organizations in promoting sustainable and democratic energy systems. However, most of this emphasis has focused on modern industrialized societies. This article reviews research on energy alternatives conceptualized and practiced by movements and communities across the Global South. Based on the surveyed literature, we propose the concept of social energy futures (SEF) as an open-ended category to reflect on the drivers and features of these alternatives. As outlined, SEF are diverse and territorially situated, commonly encompassing three components: ( a ) they are largely needs-oriented, tending to prioritize use value over exchange value; ( b ) they involve broad political processes, defining how much energy should be harvested, through which technologies, by which actors, and for which purposes; and ( c ) they are part of broader identity struggles, reflecting how social actors actively organize to counteract colonial and corporate relations amid the energy and climate crisis. Taking these findings together, we propose an SEF analytical toolkit and outline future research themes to continue developing across diverse academic, cultural, and geographical settings.

articles.title: Metric Selection Framework: A Method for Optimizing Multidimensional Value Assessment of Resource Recovery Systems
articles.authors: Eleni Iacovidou, Spyridoula Gerassimidou, Philip Purnell, Norman Ebner
articles.abstract: This article introduces the metric selection framework (MSF), developed as part of the CVORR+ methodology. CVORR+ is a systems-based evaluation toolkit designed to support complex sustainability assessment and decision-making. Within CVORR+, the MSF translates system analysis into decision-oriented, multidimensional metrics for monitoring, assessment, and evaluation of progress toward sustainability targets. Grounded in a value-focused decision-making approach, the framework combines expert elicitation with stakeholder engagement to ensure that metrics are system grounded, context specific, and practically relevant. Applied to England's plastic packaging system, the MSF reveals systemic inefficiencies, identifies leverage points for intervention, and informs policy design to support systemic value recovery. The case study demonstrates the heuristic and practical value of the MSF in capturing interdependencies across environmental, economic, social, and technical domains. Future developments will streamline the translation from system conceptualization to metric development, ensuring that metrics are responsive to long-term monitoring and policy-making, remain aligned with technological and regulatory shifts, and enhance the robustness and transferability of CVORR+.

articles.title: Between Family and Community: Intergenerational Interactions and Pathways to Active Ageing in Urban China
articles.abstract: This article examines how intergenerational interactions intersect with community resources to shape pathways to active ageing among urban older adults in China. Drawing on intergenerational solidarity theory, it conceptualises family and community as an integrated configuration in which care responsibilities and moral expectations are redistributed rather than simply shifted. Based on 40 semi‐structured interviews conducted in a subdistrict of Health Commission of Changning District Shanghai (2024), the analysis compares three residential arrangements: three‐generation co‐residence, empty‐nest households with distant children, and proximate but non‐co‐resident families (“a bowl of soup's distance”). It identifies three pathways: facilitation, where stable family support enables community participation; substitution, where community services replace routine functional support under distance; and complementarity, where proximity and community embeddedness jointly sustain autonomy. Across pathways, active ageing emerges as a moralised achievement sustained through self‐discipline, selective disclosure, and restrained help‐seeking to avoid “burdening” adult children.

articles.title: Divergent Paths of US Counties: Multiscale Drivers and Spatial Dynamics of Population Growth and Decline (2010−2020)
articles.abstract: Population change across US counties has taken sharply different paths, with some areas experiencing steady growth while others face persistent decline. These trends are not random; they reflect deeper shifts in the economy and uneven regional development. This study contributes to demographic and regional research by treating population growth and decline as two distinct demographic regimes, each influenced by its own set of factors. We examine which factors are associated with county‐level population change in the United States from 2010 to 2020, using data from 3130 counties with complete records across all explanatory variables, compiled from the American Community Survey, the Bureau of Economic Analysis and fiscal records. To capture both overall patterns and local variations, we combine standard regression methods (OLS, spatial lag and spatial error models) with Multiscale Geographically Weighted Regression (MGWR). Counties are explicitly divided into growing ( N = 1548) and shrinking ( N = 1582) groups, with models estimated separately for each. The findings show a moderate but consistent asymmetry between growth and decline. Declining counties tend to cluster together and are associated with consistent factors such as aging populations, weak labour markets, reliance on agriculture and, to a more limited extent, housing tenure. Growth, on the other hand, is more spatially variable and localized. It is associated with an agricultural employment structure operating at a broad scale, while natural increase and tax burden exhibit highly localized associations, and housing tenure shows a broader but uneven association. MGWR provides a substantially better fit than global models in both cases ( R 2 = 0.546 for growing counties and 0.595 for shrinking counties, compared with 0.043 and 0.150 under standard OLS), highlighting that population change is a complex, multiscale process. Understanding these spatial patterns is crucial for developing policies and planning strategies that are sensitive to local conditions.

articles.title: An Intersectional Theory of Gendered Political Violence Under Sectarian Systems
articles.abstract: Political violence against women is often analyzed primarily through gender, leaving underexplored how other systems of domination shape its production and enforcement. This article develops an intersectional feminist institutionalist framework to explain how patriarchal and sectarian formal and informal rules co-produce political violence against women in deeply divided societies. Drawing on Lebanon as a theory-building case study and applying an abductive approach to our empirical data, we argue that such violence is not simply a backlash against women’s political presence, but is core to preserving the sectarian order. We identify three overlapping mechanisms through which political violence against women candidates is enforced by multiple actors, namely family coercion, party- and militia-linked enforcement, and sectarian boundary policing, with all of them mobilizing scripts of honor, purity, loyalty, and communal stability to constrain women’s political agency. Our framework offers broader insights into intersectional political violence across ethnically and religiously divided societies.

articles.title: Intersecting Identities: How Gender and Disability Shape Voter Perceptions of Election Candidates
articles.abstract: Voters’ perceptions of election candidates are known to be shaped by stereotypes about candidates’ characteristics and social identities, including gender and disability. More recently, scholars have started paying attention to how the intersection of politicians’ identities shapes citizens’ perceptions of them, recognizing that identities do not simply “add up” but give rise to distinct stereotypes and expectations. This paper explores how candidate gender and disability affect voter perceptions through a survey experiment with a conjoint design in the UK and the US. The findings reveal a complex picture in which candidate gender and disability interact in shaping some, but not the majority, of voters’ perceptions of candidates’ traits, competences, beliefs, as well as voter support. The study underlines that intersectional approaches are fundamental to advancing our understanding of voter attitudes and behavior, candidate competition, and the representation of social groups.

articles.title: Executive Aggrandizement: Understanding the Silent Erosion of Democratic Constraints
articles.abstract: Studies of executive aggrandizement face a double measurement problem. Measures of aggrandizement may include institutions that constitute liberal democracy, while broad composites may treat substantively different executive practices as interchangeable. This article develops a measurement‐oriented classification that reduces direct overlap with the V‐Dem Liberal Democracy Index and compares distinct practices under common analytical rules. Using V‐Dem v15 data and a common sample of 17,404 country‐years across 179 countries from 1901 to 2024, country‐ and year‐fixed‐effects models estimate conditional within‐country associations for five lagged practices. Patronal‐distributive allocation, judicial purges, and personalist/mobilizational legitimation are negatively associated with liberal democracy. Executive corruption is consistently imprecise, whereas politicized administrative appointments are negative only in some specifications. Item‐level, restricted‐period, timing, and first‐difference analyses document practice heterogeneity but also show exceptional persistence; negative future‐lead estimates prevent a causal or sequential reading. The primary contribution is a bounded measurement and modeling strategy that preserves comparability while reducing, rather than claiming to eliminate, outcome overlap. Its linked theoretical contribution is a practice‐family account of executive aggrandizement: politically coordinated practices may coexist and remain interdependent without becoming interchangeable indicators or stages in a common causal sequence.

articles.title: Independent Agencies, Regulation‐Compliant Citizens? Evidence From a Survey Experiment on Vaccine Authorization in the EU
articles.authors: Benjamin Leidorf‐Tidå, Saar Alon‐Barkat, Madalina Busuioc, Thijs de Boer
articles.abstract: The effectiveness of regulatory policy in many areas is contingent on citizens adhering to the scientific advice of regulatory bodies. This in turn depends on whether they perceive this advice as credible . One of the biggest threats to regulatory credibility is the concern that regulatory policy can be tainted by short‐term political interests. Consequently, regulation literature points to agency independence as a crucial resource to securing regulatory credibility, which in turn fosters citizen compliance. We test this assumption both observationally and experimentally in the case of the European Medicines Agency's (EMA) risk assessment for the first COVID‐19 vaccine—a prime example of reliance on credibility in regulation under conditions of controversy and concerns over political interference. We conducted a pre‐registered survey experiment with 4000 EU citizens from four countries timed shortly after the vaccine's approval and before its mass distribution. The results provide partial support that independence is beneficial to regulatory credibility and by extension, to regulatory compliance. Citizens who perceive the EMA as more independent found its risk assessment to be more credible and were more willing to take the vaccine. However, our experimental evidence is less conclusive. Thus, while independence might not in and of itself be a “silver bullet” to ensure regulatory credibility and compliance, it does play an important role, and its real‐life substantive significance would scale up considerably at population levels.

articles.title: Linkage as Leverage: OECD Accession as an Informal and Indirect Graduation Mechanism in the International Climate Regime
articles.abstract: As global power is shifting, international institutions face a challenge: established powers will often request that rising powers no longer continue to benefit from their status as “developing countries”. Yet only a few institutions have formal rules in place to organize this transition. As a result, tracing the informal pathways through which change occurs becomes relevant. In this article, we study one such mechanism in the international climate regime. In that regime, the so‐called Annex I countries agreed “to take the lead” in reducing greenhouse gas emissions while developing countries remained exempt from a similar obligation. Because Annex I was hard to amend, the regime has frequently been said to lack a graduation mechanism. Yet, once we take the interaction between the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and its broader institutional environment into account, the process of acceding to the Organization for Economic Co‐operation and Development (OECD) comes into view as an indirect and informal graduation mechanism. We examine the effects and limitations of this mechanism in relation to the accession processes of Mexico (1994), South Korea (1996), and Chile (2010). Our analysis leads to two main results. First, we show that a graduation mechanism based on “linkage as leverage” existed. Second, we sketch three distinct causal pathways that lead to different degrees of graduation in each case. Overall, our study suggests that graduation based on “linkage as leverage” depends on three conditions. First, states needed to activate the mechanism in each case. Second, domestic support was required to sustain graduation. And third, major emitters had to develop an interest in joining a club organization that could exercise leverage.

articles.title: From Judicial Regulation to Judicial Governance: Locating the Courts on the Map of Social Ordering
articles.abstract: Courts have long been recognized as venues of social control and policymaking. The rise of regulatory capitalism suggests reconsidering the judiciary in regulatory terms, notably through work that casts courts as regulators. This article argues, however, that styling courts as regulators is both analytically and normatively deficient: it obscures the distinctive function of courts and their contribution to social ordering. At the same time, judicial decision‐making plainly exhibits a regulatory dimension. Yet rather than stretching the concept of regulation, this article proposes to capture this dimension through governance theory. On this theoretical foundation, the article outlines a model of judicial governance that elucidates how social ordering emerges from adjudication and how it unfolds over time. In particular, the model highlights the implications of judicial decision‐making for private ordering and draws attention to processes of intermediation through lawyers, media, and advanced digital technologies. It thus opens a set of analytically structured research questions and complements them with a methodological framework to orient future work on judicial governance.

articles.title: Imagining the Invisible: Judicial Epistemology, Carceral Regulation, and the Liberal State
articles.abstract: In many systems judges exercise judicial review over prison officials' decisions. However, judges are often symbolically, institutionally, and practically distant from prison realities. In the current paper, we explore how judges negotiate their limited epistemological awareness of prison through the lens of epistemic injustice. Drawing on interviews with 17 (retired) Israeli Supreme Court justices regarding their prison administrative review decisions, we identify three epistemic gaps: first, the prison's heterotopic nature; second, the tension between commitment to liberty and authorizing the “pains of imprisonment” at sentencing; and third, the division of labor between sentencing and prison phases. The findings suggest that judges bridge these epistemological gaps through three imaginaries: (a) “ epistemic distancing ”; (b) “ epistemic assimilation ”; and (c) “ parallel epistemology ”. These epistemic imaginaries allow judges to compensate for their experiential absence but also structure their judicial oversight, shaping how courts administratively regulate imprisonment without fully confronting its lived realities. The findings show how judicial imaginaries of prison are shaped through top‐down narrative constructions rather than bottom‐up experiential encounters and include self‐produced “epistemic estrangement” from the prison world. We further examine the implications of these epistemic blind spots, demonstrating how they enable the legitimization of carceral power while obscuring and marginalizing the lived experiences of incarcerated individuals.

articles.title: Economic Governance and Institutional Design
articles.abstract: How should institutions be designed to achieve compliance with behavioral rules, including laws, social norms, religious rules, or cultural traditions? This conceptual paper introduces a typology of economic governance institutions and explains how it can be used both by policy makers, administrators, and researchers in all social sciences to improve rule compliance. It explains how effective and efficient institutions can be identified for a given economic governance problem. The framework is built on the microeconomic foundations of economic governance theory, and its applicability extends to any compliance problem that can be formalized as a social dilemma or coordination game. The concepts are applied to two cases: how to create trust in cloud computing technologies, and how to implement data sharing of user‐generated information on data‐driven markets.

articles.title: Professionalizing deliberation: a Social Network Analysis of UK climate mini-publics
articles.abstract: Deliberative mini-publics have become an increasingly prominent feature of climate governance across advanced democracies. In the United Kingdom, their rapid expansion has been accompanied by the emergence of a professional deliberative field composed of facilitators, recruitment agencies, advisory bodies, expert witnesses, and network organizations. While existing scholarship debates whether professionalization enhances deliberative quality or introduces risks of marketization and elite capture, there is limited empirical evidence on how influence, standards, and authority are structured within this field. This article addresses that gap by mapping the actors involved in the design and delivery of UK climate mini-publics using qualitative social network analysis. The analysis examines how professional ties shape the circulation of expertise, standards, and backstage decision-making. The findings identify important and influential actors within the network, and their place within the wider industry. Here, we highlight the unequal concentration and clustering within the network. Rather than finding clear evidence of elite capture, the analysis reveals a form of structural dependency. Responsibility and authority are frequently transferred from commissioning bodies to facilitators, concentrating influence in a small number of actors. While these actors often act as safeguards of deliberative integrity, this reliance also introduces fragility, risks of stagnation, and uneven standards across the field. The article concludes that professionalization is neither inherently corrosive nor unproblematic. By foregrounding the networked architecture of deliberation, the study contributes a new perspective on how democratic innovations are governed, stabilized, and constrained in practice.

articles.title: Centripetal narratives under crisis? Media framing and the Europeanization of economic discourse in Portugal, Spain, and Ireland
articles.abstract: This article examines whether and how national media in Portugal, Spain, and Ireland converged in their interpretation of European economic issues during the Eurozone crisis. Building on research on the European Public Sphere, it analyses how national media located political authority, responsibility, and problem-solving capacity under conditions of intensified EU involvement in domestic economic governance. Conceptually, the article distinguishes between relational convergence, referring to cross-national similarity in media narratives, and directional convergence, capturing within-country shifts in narrative orientation along the national–EU axis. Empirically, the analysis draws on a comparative framing study of 6,070 economic news articles published in six quality newspapers between 2002 and 2015. Narrative interpretation across five framing dimensions—Problem, Cause, Responsibility, Consequences, and Solution—is operationalised through an original Convergence Index capturing the balance between EU-centred and nationally centred narratives. The findings show no generalised relational convergence following the onset of the crisis. Instead, cross-national dispersion in narrative orientation increases in the post-crisis period. Directional convergence towards EU-centred narratives occurs selectively: Spanish and Irish media display modest centripetal shifts, whereas Portuguese coverage follows a contrasting trajectory of systematic re-nationalisation. Overall, these results qualify crisis-driven expectations of communicative integration. While the Eurozone crisis intensified diagnostic and accountability-oriented framing across national media, it did not generate stable or cumulative convergence in narrative interpretation. Media convergence thus emerges as a differentiated and non-linear process, with important implications for how the communicative foundations of a European Public Sphere should be assessed under conditions of systemic stress.

articles.title: Can multi-dimensional descriptive representation increase policy priority alignment? Evidence from South African municipalities
articles.authors: Evan Lieberman, Sarah Lockwood, Philip Martin, Vinothan Naidoo
articles.abstract: Does an increase in the number of shared identity traits between citizens and their public representatives increase the likelihood that they will agree on policy priorities? The identities of citizens and politicians are complex and multi-dimensional, but we know little about how the combination of multiple shared identity traits affects the convergence of attitudes on government policy. In this paper, we analyze two waves of original survey data on local government councillors in conjunction with several surveys of citizens in South Africa. We find that both within and across political parties, greater degrees of trait similarity between citizens and politicians – even beyond the one or two traits considered in most studies of descriptive representation – are associated with modest but consistent increases in alignment on policy priorities, especially when citizens and councillors share traits that reinforce a historically marginalized identity. We also show that trait similarity increases policy priority alignment to a greater degree when politicians have roles that require frequent contact with constituents, suggesting that communication channels may strengthen the substantive impact of descriptive representation.

articles.title: Does politics drive cultural preferences? Voting behavior in the Eurovision Song Contest
articles.authors: Estelle E. Brun, Taylor C. Boas
articles.abstract: In the context of growing polarization and culture war conflict, politics is often seen as invading cultural spaces such as sports and popular music. An example is the Eurovision Song Contest (ESC), where political attitudes toward participant countries are thought to influence outcomes. In this study, we administer an online survey in four European countries to examine voting behavior in the ESC. Unlike existing studies, our individual-level data allow us to distinguish political influences on ESC voting behavior from cultural attitudes and song quality. We show that most voting in the contest is idiosyncratic, not political. Political attitudes, cultural attitudes, and song quality all influence ESC voting behavior, but effects and explained variance are small. Moreover, political attitudes only influence voting for those countries—Ukraine and Israel—whose policies generate strong opinions. The results suggest that, even in polarized contexts, cultural preferences are still primarily about aesthetics rather than politics.

articles.title: Administrative state capacity and the effect of EU democracy assistance on levels of democracy: a time-series cross-sectional analysis, 2007–2021
articles.authors: Steve Biedermann, Sonja Grimm, Karina Shyrokykh
articles.abstract: The European Union (EU) is one of the world’s major donors of democracy assistance, which aims to foster democratisation. Its effects, however, depend on various conditional factors. This study explores the nexus between democracy assistance and administrative state capacity. Since democracy assistance seeks to strengthen —not substitute—the state and its institutions, we argue that administrative capacity is a crucial condition for the effectiveness of democracy assistance. To test our argument, we conduct a time-series cross-sectional analysis covering EU democracy assistance allocation from 2007 to 2021 across 23 countries in the EU’s neighbourhood. Our results indicate that assistance allocated to countries with higher state capacity has a more substantial effect on their levels of democracy than assistance allocated to countries with lower state capacity. With that, we address an important research gap and contribute to policy debates on the allocation of democracy assistance.

articles.title: Selecting climate solutions creates new institutional authority
Enhancing fairness in climate action through policy packages
articles.authors: Toon Vandyck, Umed Temursho, Florian Landis, David Klenert, Matthias Weitzel
articles.abstract: Achieving a fair transition to climate neutrality requires a careful balancing of policy options. Here we quantitatively evaluate the equity implications of different European Union climate policy packages, considering pricing, regulation via standards, subsidies and transfers. Leveraging an integrated modelling framework, we show that standards limit impact variability within income groups, whereas carbon pricing with transfer-based revenue recycling offsets regressive impacts between income groups. Restricting climate policy implementation to either option, therefore, gives rise to a trade-off between horizontal and vertical equity. We then demonstrate numerically how a multi-instrument budget-neutral policy package can resolve this trade-off. Adopting a broader equity perspective that encompasses both horizontal and vertical equity shifts the preferred policy mix towards a combination of standards, pricing, subsidies and transfers. These results provide an explicit, quantified, equity-based rationale for the adoption and acceptability of comprehensive climate policy packages, offering a more nuanced view on policy design.

articles.title: Citizens’ assemblies propose ambitious climate policy but impacts remain limited
articles.authors: Janosch Pfeffer, Hannah Einhauser, Johanna Hauke, Kira Hoffmann, Lisa Ruf, Milena Weber, Florian Weckbecker, Marlene Wellhausen, Jens Newig
articles.abstract: Climate citizens’ assemblies convene randomly selected citizens who, after structured learning and deliberation, develop policy recommendations. Yet, whether they produce more ambitious recommendations and influence political decisions remains contested. Here we conduct a comparative, counterfactual assessment of 488 recommendations from five national and one state-level assembly in Western Europe, drawing on document analysis and expert interviews. The results show that citizens consistently proposed more ambitious climate measures than existing government policy. Recommendations sometimes influenced policy by adding momentum, enriching plans, breaking deadlocks or introducing novel ideas, but such influence was rare. Only the French assembly shows substantial policy impact, with one-third of its recommendations having influenced policy, due to strong power delegation, political leadership and resulting public pressure. In the other cases, policy impact was minimal or absent. These findings show that citizens’ assemblies can raise policy ambition, but translating recommendations into political decisions depends strongly on political conditions.

articles.title: Television Time and Electoral Success: Evidence From the Constitutional Convention Election in Chile in 2021
articles.abstract: Some democracies give all political parties free television time to level the electoral campaign playing field. Relying on a case that uses open-list proportional representation rules and where voters select individual candidates, but where free television time is assigned to party lists, we explore the association between appearing in free television ads (franja) and electoral success in Chile’s 2021 Constitutional Convention election. In this unprecedented contest, airtime was allocated to parties and lists of independents. We use an original coding of 3,157 mentions across 28 days of television ads for candidates in the four largest electoral lists (692 candidates). Candidates mentioned in ads received higher vote shares (2.9 vs. 2.2 percent) and were more likely to win seats (18.6 vs. 7.7 percent). Multivariate models show that campaign spending is more strongly associated with electoral success, but mentions in the franja have a modest but statistically significant positive coefficient. Although we cannot disentangle the potential endogeneity of being more electable and appearing in the franja, the findings highlight the importance of television time for electoral success and point to how party-controlled media exposure influences intra-list competition.

articles.title: How Personal Curation Shapes Political Engagement on Social Media? Examining The Politics of Personal Curation Model
articles.abstract: Although individuals today have a wide range of media choices to engage in politics, recent investigations have revealed that many are increasingly avoiding news and disengaging from politics, especially in social media. From a user-centered perspective, few effective strategies on social media have been systematically examined to enhance political engagement. Established through the curated flows framework, this study proposes the Politics of Personal Curation (PPC) model, which offers a fresh perspective by examining how everyday mundane personal curation in social media (platform expansiveness, content heterogeneity, news attentiveness, and source belongingness curation) have significantly influences on political engagement. A preregistered study from a nationally representative panel in the United States ( N = 1,270) generally indicates that expansiveness, heterogeneity, and news attentiveness curation yield higher political engagement, whereas belongingness curation is linked to lower engagement. This study further supports that these media effects on political engagement are channeled through enhanced cognitive elaboration and moderated by cross-cutting discussion.

articles.title: Understanding Early Attitudes Towards Generative AI Regulation in Higher Education: The Role of Academic Scientists’ Experience and Risk Perceptions
articles.authors: Jinghuan Ma, Tipeng Chen, Rong Zuo, Timothy P. Johnson, Eric W. Welch, Ashlee Frandell, Wenceslao Arroyo‐Machado, Lesley Michalegko
articles.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technology rapidly permeates higher education, it creates opportunities to transform teaching, research, and workforce preparation while raising ethical, social and environmental concerns. Academic scientists have a unique role in this transition as their early exposure to publicly accessible GenAI tools shapes emerging practices, norms, and institutional responses. Existing research often treats AI‐related risk as a single construct, limiting understanding of how distinct risk dimensions shape regulatory preferences. This study investigates how academic scientists’ experience with GenAI relates to risk perceptions over agency loss and data breach, and how these perceptions are associated with their regulatory attitudes during its formative stage. Using survey data collected between September and November 2023, shortly after ChatGPT became widely accessible, we find that greater GenAI experience is associated with lower perceived risks. Meanwhile, different risk perceptions are linked to distinct regulatory preferences: perceived risk of agency loss is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation and a lower likelihood of supporting academic self‐regulation, whereas perceived data breach risk is associated with a greater likelihood of supporting federal regulation but not associated with the likelihood of supporting self‐regulation. These findings provide an early baseline understanding of faculty attitudes toward GenAI regulation in academic contexts.

articles.title: Gambling Advertising and Problem Gambling in the United States: Multi‐Level Evidence Beyond Sports‐Betting Legal Status
articles.authors: Chris J. Vargo, Toby Hopp, Harsha Gangadharbatla
articles.abstract: US gambling debates often center on the legal status of sports‐betting, but advertising can also be used as a distinct policy lever. This paper presents the findings of two related studies. Study 1 links quarterly state‐level gambling advertising outlays across paid media (2014–2023) to Google Trends indices for 116 problem‐gambling help‐seeking queries across 41 states (1640 state‐quarters). Study 2 combines surveys with passive digital traces from 419 exposure‐eligible mobile‐platform users. Higher state‐level ad spend, but not sports‐betting legal status, was associated with greater help‐seeking search interest, and this association strengthened over time. Platform‐specific gambling‐ad exposure on Facebook, TikTok, and X was associated with gambler status, gambling frequency, and the probability of any observed gambling‐site visit. Clean gambling ads were also associated with higher 24‐h odds of subsequent gambling touchpoints, especially web visits; among gamblers, ad‐triggered touchpoints were associated with problem‐gambling scores more consistently than raw clean ad volume. Convergent state‐level and individual‐level evidence links gambling advertising with engagement and harm‐related indicators, while the observational designs do not identify causal effects. The findings support stronger restrictions on advertising volume, placement, inducements, and targeting.
