articles.title: Love of variety? An experimental study of heterogeneous responses to foreign brands in the marketplace
articles.abstract: Do everyday encounters with foreign brands shape political attitudes? We argue that brand origin cues activate national identities, producing different responses among nationalists and cosmopolitans. In an online shopping experiment, U.S. participants were randomly assigned to compare American (control), European, or Asian (treatment) sport utility vehicles without explicit mention of brand origin. Exposure to foreign brands increased opposition to trade and immigration and support for Donald Trump among nationalists. Cosmopolitans generally showed little change. These effects are not reducible to partisanship, revealing within-coalition divides among Republicans and among Democrats and Independents. Our findings show that subtle consumer experiences spill over into politics, creating a bottom-up channel of polarization that links nationalism and populism to support for neomercantilist and nativist policies.

articles.title: How Do (Mis-)Perceptions of Refugee Gender Composition Shape Attitudes? Evidence from a Survey Experiment
articles.authors: Andrea Blasco, Michal Krawczyk, Hannah Nohlen
articles.abstract: People’s perceptions of others, particularly those from other countries, can shape their attitudes and willingness to offer solidarity. We study public beliefs about the gender composition of forcibly displaced populations in a large online survey experiment. Participants ( n = 13,008) representative of the adult population of six EU countries, consistently underestimated the share of women among the people displaced by the Russian war on Ukraine. We show that a belief-correction intervention effectively prompted updates in public beliefs, aligning them more closely with actual numbers. The source of information matters: updates were greater when the intervention cites official statistics rather than other people’s opinions. Although female migrants are typically preferred, the intervention did not change perceptions regarding current refugees’ impact on crime and economy or policy preferences (family reunification). While all these measures correlate with beliefs about gender composition, the intervention did not significantly affect any of them.

articles.title: Using Television Drama to Promote Electoral Corruption Reporting: An Evaluation in Northern Nigeria
articles.authors: Dan Brown, Ariel Lee Bothen, Michelle Krieger, Fatima Turaki, Mansur Kurugu, Maji Peterx, Catherine Angai, Ummi Yakubu, Vanessa Alli
articles.abstract: We evaluated an edutainment intervention to encourage electoral corruption reporting in northern Nigeria via a live broadcast of a popular Hausa-language TV show, which aired October–December 2022, shortly before the February 2023 presidential elections. We incorporated behaviorally informed anticorruption messages into the scripts of the TV drama to encourage its tens of millions of viewers to report instances of electoral corruption. We used a randomized encouragement trial design, sampling over 6,000 participants across northern Nigeria through pre-recorded phone surveys. Watching the show caused a statistically significant increase in the perceived helpfulness and frequency of reporting, but we could not detect changes in knowledge of how to report or reporting behaviors.

articles.title: Covariate Adjustment in Political Science Experiments: Progress and Recommendations
articles.abstract: Covariate adjustment can reduce the standard error of experimental treatment effect estimates without increasing the sample size but is vulnerable to abuse unless a specific procedure is preregistered. We assess adjustment practices in ten political science journals in 2013, 2018, and 2023–24. Encouragingly, preregistration and covariate adjustment have each been rapidly adopted. Preregistration is also a good predictor of what practices are used in articles. However, just 12% of articles published in 2023–24 preregister a specific covariate adjustment procedure and use adjustment for the main estimate. Although preregistering an adjusted estimator is not always advisable (when covariates are unavailable or preregistration is not possible), there is substantial room for improvement. We recommend that when feasible, researchers preregister a specific covariate adjustment procedure and use it for their preferred estimate regardless of covariate balance. This may require a shift in preregistration culture away from predicting results and toward constraining analysis.

articles.title: Perceiving Politics: Considering the Political Categorization of Faces
articles.authors: Thomas Bergeron, Blake Lee-Withing, Natasha Goel
articles.abstract: Categorizing people into groups is a fundamentally human trait, but we know very little about how people assign political identities to strangers. Across two innovative survey experiments, we consider how people politically categorize others according to a single source of information: faces. We find that displays of emotions, particularly negative emotions, predict the political sorting of strangers. Faces featuring negative emotions are categorized as out-partisans, whereas faces exhibiting happiness are categorized as co-partisans.

articles.title: Big Tech, big risk? How education and ideology shape public attitudes toward Big Tech companies
articles.authors: Tobias Tober, Marius R. Busemeyer, Sebastian Koos
articles.abstract: This paper examines public attitudes toward Big Tech and their relationship to policy preferences in six OECD countries. Drawing on original survey data collected in 2022 from 19,800 respondents in Germany, Japan, Poland, Spain, Sweden, and the United States, we analyze how education and political ideology shape evaluations of large technology firms such as Google, Apple, Meta, Amazon, and Microsoft. Using six survey items on the perceived economic, social, and democratic effects of Big Tech, we identify two weakly correlated attitudinal dimensions: positive and negative evaluations. A cluster analysis reveals five groups of respondents—supporters, skeptics, ambivalent, dismissive, and neutral—highlighting that public opinion on Big Tech is not organized along a single continuum. Bayesian multinomial regression models show that higher education is associated less with outright support than with greater ambivalence, while ideology structures attitudes in distinct ways: skepticism is more pronounced on the left, whereas ambivalence rises especially among highly educated respondents on the right. These attitudinal clusters are closely linked to preferences for regulation and government support. The findings suggest that public opinion toward Big Tech is complex, politically structured, and consequential for policy debates.

articles.title: Webs of Ainu Mosir: Indigenous Creative Networks on YouTube
articles.authors: Xanat Vargas Meza, Takumi Yokoyama, Chieko Nishimura, Ryohei Nishida, Yoichi Ochiai
articles.abstract: The Ainu are Indigenous people living primarily in Japan. As they have recently adopted social media, and network-based analyses of First Nations cultural manifestations are uncommon, this study drew on Indigenous and social network frameworks to examine creative networks in the virtual Mosir (the world as viewed by the Ainu). Our objective was to clarify the types of collaborators, their cooperation patterns and relationships relevant to producing Ainu-related YouTube videos. Three YouTube lists of 428 videos were utilised in this study. Publicly available data were downloaded using a YouTube Application Programming Interface (API). The videos were watched and classified, including anonymised data on collaborators. The relationships of the collaborators were quantified and mapped, network measurements were calculated and collaborator clusters were examined. The most frequent types of collaborators were individuals and communities. We also observed that individuals moderately affected network clustering ( p = .002). Furthermore, individuals were somewhat correlated with the average number of ties ( p = .004) and the bridging of clusters through betweenness ( p = .006), with Japanese male celebrities and Ainu people, particularly Ainu women, showing high centrality. As Indigenous rights advance internationally, the virtual Mosir shows how crucial it is for First Nations to participate in multimedia production processes, particularly if such productions are available on social media. Indigenous network frameworks were highly compatible with network analysis, allowing for a more comprehensive overview of Indigenous production processes. This can enhance the multiple knowledges of First Nations, while fostering accountability and reciprocity of their allies.

articles.title: Careful Dis/Connection: Bringing Digital (Inter)Dependent Relations Out From the Shadows of Autonomy
articles.abstract: Although always-on connectivity affords autonomy, it also creates dependencies on digital devices. Digital disconnection has emerged as a countermovement, with people seeking ‘authentic’ offline reconnection under the discourse of (self-)care. Yet, a pertinent question is whether certain care relations are contingent on digital dependencies between people and, despite being perceived as burdensome, should therefore not be broken through disconnection. Drawing on feminist ethics of care, which understands care as all the work that maintains everyday life, this article examines how care and digital dis/connection practices shape each other. Empirically, it draws on ethnographic fieldwork with 20 adults and analyses three vignettes through a relational framework that follows care occurring in, through and away from digital devices. The findings show that digital well-being is shaped less by individual media use than by the care relations that digital technologies sustain. Experiences of digital dis/connection reveal how connectivity is embedded in often invisible responsibilities, dependencies, and forms of care. Rather than locating digital tensions in technologies themselves, the analysis suggests that such tensions expose underlying challenges in how care is organised, valued, and distributed. In response, the article develops the framework of careful dis/connection to evaluate digital practices according to how they sustain, redistribute, and make visible the care on which everyday life depends.

articles.title: Algorithms of Injustice: An Ethnographic Content Analysis of Black Youth’s Experiences with Racial Trauma Online
articles.abstract: This study explores the pervasive presence of racially traumatic content (RTC) on social media and its profound impact on the mental well-being of Black youth. Utilizing ethnographic content analysis and grounded in critical race technology theory (CRTT), the research identifies key manifestations of RTC, including Black death, digital harassment, deepfakes, and war content. Social media’s algorithmic structures amplify RTC, perpetuating systemic anti-Black racism while exposing Black youth to vicarious trauma, anxiety, and depression. Despite these challenges, social media platforms also provide spaces for activism and community-building. Black youth use these digital arenas to engage in social justice narratives, find solidarity, and develop coping strategies. The findings emphasize the critical roles of educators and counselors in mitigating the adverse effects of RTC by fostering media literacy, digital resilience, and culturally responsive mental health support. This research contributes to evidence-based interventions aimed at empowering Black youth to navigate digital spaces safely, advocate for systemic change, and thrive in an equitable and inclusive online environment.

articles.title: Automated Influence: How Social Bots Reshape Discursive Opportunities in Online Activism
articles.abstract: Social bots are an increasingly prominent presence in online protest discourse. We adapt the discursive opportunity structure (DOS) framework for digital protest, refining its dimensions of visibility, resonance and legitimacy to account for platform-mediated discourse and automated activity. Applying the refined framework through computer-assisted content analysis of bot activity in two major protests – Black Lives Matter (BLM) and Extinction Rebellion (XR) – we move beyond treating bots as a monolithic or uniformly disruptive force, identifying competing pro- and counter-protest strategies distributed differently across the three dimensions. In BLM, pro-protest bot content concentrates on cultural resonance, whereas counter-bot content targets legitimacy; in XR, pro-protest bots are used to build legitimacy and participatory visibility, whereas counter-bots more often work to downplay the movement’s salience. The framework’s granularity discriminates between movement types in ways coarser accounts of ‘political bots’ cannot, showing that understanding contemporary movements requires attending to how automated activity is deployed within their discourse.

articles.authors: Yilin Zhuo, Kristin Turney, Naomi F. Sugie, M. Keith Chen, Emily Owens
articles.abstract: Social isolation is a major public health crisis with particularly deleterious consequences for vulnerable populations including incarcerated people. Theoretically, visitation from family should reduce social isolation and improve outcomes among incarcerated people, but existing quasi-experimental research provides limited support for the relationship between visitation and in-custody outcomes. We revisit the effect of visitation on in-custody misconduct—an important but administratively defined measure of institutional safety—by exploiting the fact that fluctuations in gasoline prices create unanticipated shifts in visitation uncorrelated with other factors associated with misconduct. We combine this quasi-experimental variation with smartphone mobility data identifying prison visits from cell phone pings and administrative data on misconduct in California prisons. We find that increases in visits induced by changes in transportation costs are negatively related to misconduct (particularly use-of-force events and personal battery), with effects concentrated immediately after visitation. Although the policy implications are subtle, these findings suggest that some strategies that reduce visitation barriers could be cost-effective ways to reduce prison violence. More broadly, they suggest that social connections have causal repercussions for violence and safety in extreme institutional environments.

articles.title: The network structure of the urban revolution
articles.abstract: Long-distance interaction has deep prehistoric roots, but the networks that emerged during the Urban Revolution were unprecedented in scale and organization. How early cities sustained this extensive connectivity in the absence of formal markets or centralized states remains a fundamental question. Focusing on the Uruk Expansion in Mesopotamia (ca. 3900 to 3000 BCE), we assemble the largest spatial dataset currently available and reconstruct transportation networks across three successive phases. Using network analysis, we show that an initially dendritic, river-based system evolved into modular regional clusters and ultimately into a more integrated structure linked by selective long-distance shortcuts. This transformation reduced dependence on key intermediaries and generated small world–like patterns combining strong local cohesion with efficient system-wide reach. These results demonstrate that decentralized interaction processes, supported in part by mobile intermediary communities, played a central role in sustaining early urban connectivity.

articles.title: Skill and spatial mismatches for sustainable development in Brazil
articles.authors: Anna K. Berryman, Fernanda Senra de Moura, Joris Bücker, Pete Barbrook-Johnson, Marek Hanusch, Penny Mealy, J. Doyne Farmer, R. Maria del Rio-Chanona
articles.abstract: Deforestation is a major source of global greenhouse gas emissions, and continued forest loss risks pushing the Amazon from a carbon sink to a carbon source. While recent work shows that productivity-led structural transformation towards less land-intensive sectors can reduce deforestation, the labour market implications of such pathways remain poorly understood. Here we address this gap by developing a spatially and occupationally explicit agent-based labour market model informed by empirically observed job-transition networks to simulate the ability of workers to respond to labour demand shocks. Our analysis reveals significant skill and geographic mobility frictions that constrain workers’ ability to adapt to structural change. Applying the model to productivity-driven development scenarios, we find that pathways delivering the largest deforestation and emission reductions disproportionately benefit high-skill workers while increasing unemployment among agricultural and other low-skill workers. Mobility-enhancing labour market policies can mitigate these effects, highlighting the importance of understanding labour market dynamics for equitable and feasible deforestation-reducing development pathways.

articles.title: Quantifying assets for the geopolitics of climate change mitigation
articles.authors: Guanna Pan, Ulrike Kornek, Chen Chris Gong, Edna Johanna Molina Bacca, Gunnar Luderer, Ottmar Edenhofer
articles.abstract: Climate change mitigation reshapes the distribution of economic assets in the low-carbon transition. Here we quantify climate-related assets for 169 countries across four dimensions: fossil fuel production, climate change damages, renewable energy potential and land carbon sequestration capacity. We combine integrated assessment models, climate projections, economic damage functions and biosphere datasets to assess asset changes under multiple mitigation scenarios. Geopolitical challenges and opportunities arise from climate change mitigation because losses and gains across energy and environmental assets are country-specific, which we further characterize through a broad clustering and a detailed pairwise similarity analysis. Our analysis suggests comparatively moderate impacts for the USA, the European Union and China, highlighting the challenge that the largest economic powers may not be those with the strongest asset-based interest for climate action. While our framework remains limited, our data provide input for integrating other ethical, governance and socioeconomic factors in future analyses of opportunities and challenges for ambitious climate change mitigation.
